newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Essar sees rupee gaining further vs dollar.
newsitem.headline: India's Essar sees rupee gaining further vs dollar.

text.p: The Indian rupee is poised strengthen further against the dollar in the near-term, the head of currency trading at Essar Group, one of India's top private businesses, said on Friday.
"The rupee could test further higher levels - even 35.65," N.S. Paramasivam, vice president (forex) of Essar Group of firms, told Reuters.
The rupee jumped to 35.75 against the dollar last week after being stuck close to 35.85 for most of the past six months. The rupee was trading at 35.745/752 in late Friday morning deals.
"The rupee has only to appreciate -- up to what level the RBI (Reserve Bank of India) will tolerate is difficult to say," Paramasivam said.
The RBI had capped the rupee's rise at 35.80/90 level from July 1996 to March 1997.
This month the central bank appeared to loosen its grip on the exchange rate, as intervention caused money supply expansion and aggravated overliquidity in the banking system.
But it has not backed away from the market completely, and some dealers said RBI intervention had braked the rupees rise at around 35.75 this week.
And despite the recent gains Paramasivam said the RBI has not let go of the reins recent on the rupee.
"A 10-paise gain can't be viewed as a let-go policy by the RBI," Paramasivam said.
The RBI could be testing the market, he said. "Another 10 paise gain may not attract any serious intervention from RBI."
But the pressure on the rupee to rise meant the currency should appreciate.
"The net dollar supply is too large," said Paramasivam, whose Essar Group, with interests in steel, telecommunications, oil and power, recorded sales of over 46 billion rupees last year.
Heavy capital inflows are feeding the supply of dollars and Indian importers have virtually stopped covering forward positions because of the one-way traffic in the rupee, he said.
"A sharp drop in forward premiums is more worrisome for exporters rather than the 10 paise appreciation in the spot rate," Paramasivam said.
Six-month annualised forward dollar premium breached the 5.0 percent mark in recent weeks for the first time since September 1995, dealers said.

Exporters are selling forward dollars to take advantage of the prevailing premiums at a time when interest rates are falling because of steps taken by the RBI in its 1997/98 (April-March) monetary and credit policy, dealers said.
India's large capital inflows stem from foreign direct investment as well as foreign institutional investment in Indian stocks.
A slowdown in Indian imports, reducing demand for dollars, further aided the rupee's rise.
